Costner reportedly invested $38 million of his own money in the project. When the first film underperformed, the planned theatrical release of Chapter 2 was postponed, leaving the future of the larger saga less certain.

The important caveat is that Horizon was never simply a Yellowstone spin-off. Costner had been developing the project for decades, long before his television success. He has also said that he made the film for people who appreciate his work on Yellowstone, describing it as a continuation of his relationship with that audience.

Ultimately, Costner needs the audience that John Dutton helped build, but he also needs to prove that people will follow him beyond John Dutton. A familiar star can get people interested in a new franchise; compelling storytelling, word of mouth and a satisfying payoff are what persuade them to keep coming back.

title: New Dover Towpath offers hike through Morris Canal history
fullText:
Dover officials will gather along a remnant of the Morris Canal Saturday to celebrate the town's rich history and the opening of a new recreational trail.

The nearly mile-long Dover Towpath is a stitch in a much-larger effort to remake the legendary canal's route into a pedestrian greenway stretching from the Hudson River to the Delaware.

Town officials will cut a ceremonial ribbon at Waterworks Park to open a restored portion of the path where mules once hauled barges up and down the waterway. The canal served as a critical transportation artery in North Jersey from before the Industrial Revolution until railroads and trucks put it out of business in the early 20th century.

Seasonal temperatures and blue skies are forecast for the family-friendly event, which will run from 11:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. at 100 Princeton Avenue, off the Rockaway River. A free picnic will include hot dogs, burgers and other refreshments, and a petting zoo will be part of the entertainment.

Dover's stitch in Morris Canal Greenway

The Dover portion of the towpath is envisioned as part of the Morris Canal Greenway, a 111-mile walking and bicycle trail that's still being assembled across six North Jersey counties from the Delaware on the west to the Hudson on the east.

The project "is transforming our northern New Jersey communities into more pedestrian-friendly, environmentally conscious areas, all while reducing our dependency on cars," said Dover Mayor James Dodd. "As the mayor of one of the most densely populated towns in our county, we envision a community that focuses on and emphasizes these initiatives while celebrating our history, and this is just the start."

Several segments of the Greenway have already been completed, but much work remains to create a continuous trail," according to the Canal Society of New Jersey, which is based in Stanhope.

The Dover Towpath will connect to a trail in Wharton and hopefully encourage more use of the underutilized Waterworks Park, Dover officials said.

Funded in part by a $50,000 T-Mobile grant, officials worked with the Morris County Park Commission and local students in the Dover College Promise program to design and build the towpath. The Canal Society provided an additional $10,000 grant to cover the costs and donated historical signage.

Morris Canal history

The canal was constructed from 1825 to 1831 to transport coal from Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley to customers in New Jersey and New York.

Built by the Morris Canal & Banking Co., the 102-mile waterway "would pass through the heart of New Jersey’s iron district and provide the long-needed transportation system that would create new commercial activity and enable rustic settlements like Dover and Rockaway to grow into thriving industrial towns," according to the Canal Society's website.

By the 1880s, however, railroads had rendered canals obsolete. The automobile struck the final blow, and the Morris Canal was formally abandoned in 1924.

Since then, portions of the channel have been dismantled or destroyed. But some towpaths and other historical remnants have been preserved or repurposed. Approximately 20 miles of path are planned for or already exist in Passaic County. Last year, Newark was awarded a $769,000 state grant for the second phase of the Newark Morris Canal Bikeway project. 

The North Jersey Transportation Planning Authority, in partnership with the Canal Society and the Morris Canal Working Group have presented a plan for a continuous trail that closely follows the historic canal route. The greenway would begin in Phillipsburg, end in Jersey City and in between run through Morris, Sussex, Warren, Passaic, Essex and Hudson counties.

title: Fourth of July local fireworks shows list for 2024 in North Jersey
fullText:
Independence Day will be here before we know it, so it's time to start planning how you'd like to celebrate. And, while attending a family gathering or a backyard barbecue could be fun, there's nothing quite like ringing in the Fourth of July with some fireworks, parades, festivals and more.

Because North Jersey has celebrations taking place in every corner of the region, we've compiled a list of the currently scheduled events to make your life easier.

And you won't want to miss the the 48th Annual Macy's Fourth of July Fireworks. While this event is technically in New York City, the Macy's July 4th fireworks will take place on the Hudson River for the first time since 2013, meaning New Jersey residents can view them from places like Hoboken, Jersey City and Weehawken. The show begins at 8 p.m.

Here's a look at the Fourth of July events and firework shows taking place across North Jersey in 2024, by location.

Want to see them filtered by date? Head on over to our other story: When are North Jersey fireworks?

Bergen County

Cresskill

4th of July Townwide Celebration. On July 4 (rain date July 5), enjoy a day of fun, food, rides, games, a D.J. and more. Call the Recreation Office at 201-816-8065 or jmitchell@cresskillboro.org for information. Cresskill residents only. Hours: 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Go: Community Center, 100 Third St.

East Rutherford

Meadowlands Fireworks & Fan Appreciation Night. At Fan Appreciation Night at Meadowlands Racetrack on July 6you enjoy $1 concession items, $2 Bud and Bud Light drafts, as well as a free fireworks show for July 4th after the races. Hours: 6 to 11:30 p.m. Go: Meadowlands Racetrack, 1 Racetrack Drive, East Rutherford.

Edgewater

Independence Day Fireworks. Fireworks, live music, food trucks and kids activities on June 27. Bring a chair or blanket. Parking is limited, so attendees are encouraged to use the free River Road shuttle bus. The rain date is June 30. Hours: 6 to 10 p.m. Fireworks begin at approximately 9:20. Go: Veterans Field, 1057-1165 River Road.

Fair Lawn

Fair Lawn Fireworks Show. Fair Lawn will be hosting their annual fireworks show on June 27. In addition to fireworks, there will be food vendors and live music for guests to enjoy. Tickets for the pre-fireworks festivities are $5 for children under 12 and seniors, $7 for adults and $25 for a family of five. Hours: Gates for the event open at 6:45 p.m., and fireworks begin at sundown. Go: Memorial Park, Berdan Avenue and 1st Street, Fair Lawn.

Glen Rock

Pops Celebrates Nation’s Birthday. The Pops Orchestra goes patriotic on July 3 with a free concert on the lawn of Borough Hall. Bring chairs and blankets, and enjoy the music that will include an evening of marches, popular patriotic songs and light classics under the baton of music director Anthony LaGruth. Meet the grand marshals – Marcia, Walter and Daniel Perry - of the July 4 parade as well. The IDA raffle drawing will take place during the intermission, with prizes including a $500 Visa gift card and a $250 Shop the Rock basket of gift cards from town merchants. Tickets will be available for purchase at Kilroy’s prior to the concert or at Borough Hall that night. Hours: Concert begins at 7 p.m. Go: Borough Hall, 1 Harding Plaza.

Here Comes the Parade on July 4th. Rain or shine, there will be marching bands, pipers, historic Civil War reenactors, floats, clowns and more. For information, write to grparade@icloud.com. Hours: The parade kicks off at 9:30 a.m. Go: The route begins at Glen Rock High School, 400 Hamilton Ave., and goes east on Harristown Road, takes a left on Highland Road, another left at Rock Road through the center of town, and a right on Doremus Avenue, ending at the Municipal Pool parking lot.

Leonia

Bergen County's Star-Spangled Spectacular. This Independence Day celebration on July 4 will feature the New Jersey Wind Symphony, other live entertainment, children's activities, food trucks, a beer and wine garden and fireworks at Overpeck Creek. Hours: Starts at 5 p.m. Go: Overpeck County Park, 40 Fort Lee Road, Leonia.

Lyndhurst

Lyndhurst's Zappy Fourth of July. At the Lyndhurst Band Shell, there will be a free concert on July 4 with several different performers to celebrate the Fourth of July. Hours: 7:30 to 9 p.m. Go: Lyndhurst Municipal Park, 367 Valley Brook Ave., Lyndhurst.

Paramus

Paramus 4th of July Fireworks Show. Paramus will be hosting their annual 4th of July fireworks show on June 30. Prior to the fireworks show, there will be live entertainment and food vendors. Hours: The time of the event is to be determined. Go: Cliff Gennarelli Sports Complex, Garden State Plaza Parkway, Paramus.

Paramus Independence Day Parade. The annual Independence Day Parade in Paramus on July 4 will feature participates like local first responders, community organizations and more. Hours: Begins at 9 a.m. Go: Starts at the intersection of Farview Avenue and E. Century Road, moving north on Farview Avenue. It will conclude at the Memorial Elementary School on Midland Avenue.

Ridgefield

Ridgefield Park July 4th Celebration. Ridgefield Park will have festivities all day on July 4th, including a reading of the Declaration of Independence, a flag raising ceremony and a parade. Hours: Starts at 7:30 a.m. Go: Memorial Plaza 554 Shaler Blvd., Ridgefield Park.

Ridgewood

Ridgewood 114th Annual Fourth of July Celebration. This all-day event on July 4th features a flag raising at Wilsey Square followed by a parade starting at Monroe Street and Godwin Avenue. Then, there will be evening entertainment, food trucks and a beer garden at Veterans Field, followed by the National Anthem and a fireworks show. Hours: Flag raising begins at 9 a.m.; parade begins at 10 a.m.; evening entertainment begins at 6 p.m.; and the National Anthem and fireworks begin at 9 p.m. Go: Veterans Field, 156-158 Northern Parkway, Ridgewood.

River Edge

River Edge July 4th Parade and Celebration. The events will include a parade on July 4 throughout River Edge, as well as a fair with a variety of vendors. Hours: Starts at 11 a.m. Go: Parade begins on Cherry Hill and ends at Memorial Park on Continental Avenue.

More: Fourth of July events in North Jersey kick off June 26. Here's where to catch them all

Morris County

Dover

Dover July 4th Fireworks and Celebration. Dover will be hosting a July 4th celebration with food, activities, live entertainment and fireworks on July 3. Hours: Starts at 6 p.m. Go: 302 E. McFarlan St., Dover.

Florham Park

Florham Park July 4th Celebration. During this full day of celebration on July 4, there will be a flag raising ceremony at the Florham Park Fire Department at 315 Brooklake Road, followed by the annual town parade. Then, rides, food, games and more will be available at Emmett Park Field, with fireworks in the evening. Hours: 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Go: Emmett Park Field, 111 Ridgedale Ave., Florham Park.

Hanover

Hanover Township Patriotic Celebration. Hanover Township is holding their 2024 Patriotic Celebration, which will feature food trucks, live music, games, face painting, balloon art and fireworks. Hours: 6 to 10 p.m. Go: Hanover Township Municipal Complex, 1000 Route 10, Whippany.

Lake Hopatcong

Lake Hopatcong Annual Fourth of July Fireworks. The Lake Hopatcong Yacht Club will be hosting their annual July 4th fireworks on June 28 on the main lake of Lake Hopatcong. Parking will be available on Bertrand Island for residents and members only. Hours: 9:30 to 10:30 p.m. Go: 75 North Bertrand Road, Mount Arlington.

Montville

Montville 4th of July Celebration. From June 26 through June 28, Montville will be hosting their annual 4th of July celebration events. Each day features different attractions, including food and beer trucks, carnival rides, live entertainment, a car show and fireworks. Hours: Open 5 to 10 p.m. each day. Go: Montville Township High School, 100 Horseneck Road, Montville.

Morris Plains

Morris Plains Family Day and Fireworks. The annual Morris Plains Family Day will be held at Morris Plains Community Park on June 29, featuring food, activities and entertainment. Then, their July 4th fireworks show will take place after sundown. Hours: Family Day begins at 5 p.m., and the fireworks begin around 9:30 p.m. Go: 51 Jim Fear Dr., Morris Plains.

Mountain Lakes

Mountain Lakes July 4th Fireworks. A festive July 4th fireworks show will take place July 2 over Mountain Lake, and Island Beach will be open for viewing. Hours: Starts at 9 p.m. Go: 276 Boulevard, Mountain Lakes.

Randolph

Randolph Freedom Festival. Held from July 11 to 13, the Randolph Freedom Festival will feature live music, games, food, a beer garden and fireworks. Hours: 6 to 11 p.m. Go: 214 Center Grove Road, Randolph.

Passaic County

Bloomingdale

Bloomingdale July 4th Fireworks. Bloomingdale will host their annual July 4th fireworks show on June 29 at Walter T. Bergen School. The event will also feature food and rides. Hours: Starts at 6 p.m. Go: 225 Glenwild Ave., Bloomingdale.

Clifton

Clifton Independence Day Celebration. The event on July 6 will feature a festival with food vendors, activities, games, rides, music and more, followed by a fireworks show. Hours: Starts at 4 p.m. Go: 350 Piaget Ave., Clifton.

Paterson

Paterson Food Truck Festival and Fireworks. Visitors are invited to enjoy food from local businesses, as well as a fireworks display, on June 30. Hours: Starts at 5 p.m. Go: Great Falls Welcome Center, 65 McBride Ave. Extension.

Sussex County

Augusta

July 4th Hometown Heroes Parade and Sussex County Miners Game. In Augusta on July 4, events include the Hometown Heroes Parade, a game between the Sussex County Miners and the New Jersey Jackals, as well as a fireworks display. Hours: Starts at 4:30 p.m. Go: 94 Championship Place, Augusta.

Montague

Montague Day and July 4th Fireworks. Montague Day on June 29 will feature the Miss Montague Contest, an animal exhibit, live entertainment, a cornhole tournament, a dunk tank, vendors, food, fireworks after dark and more. Hours: The event starts at 4 p.m., and the fireworks begin after dark. Go: Montague Town Hall, 227 Clover Road, Montague.

Essex County

Bloomfield

Essex County Summer Concert Series and Fireworks. Listen to the Infernos at Brookdale Park, and enjoy a fireworks show, on July 3. The Infernos’ repertoire includes big band, oldies, Motown and today’s chart hits. Founded by the late Bobby Wells, former musical director of the Duprees, the band features lead singer Kenny Simmons, formerly of the Commodores. Hours: Starts at 7:30 p.m. Go: 473 Watchung Ave., Bloomfield.

Cedar Grove

Cedar Grove Annual Fireworks Display. Cedar Grove is hosting their annual Fourth of July fireworks display and celebration event July 1, which features a live DJ, a balloon artist, a patriotic obstacle course, crafts and refreshments. Hours: Starts at 7 p.m. Go: Panther Park Field, 118 W Bradford Ave., Cedar Grove.

Livingston

Livingston July 4th Community Celebration. This all-day event on July 4 will feature a car show, food trucks, games, live entertainment and a beer garden. The celebration will conclude with Livingston's annual fireworks show. Hours: 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Go: Memorial Oval, Robert H. Harp Drive, Livingston.

Montclair

Montclair July 4th celebrations. The series of celebrations taking place in Montclair on July 4th include the town's 68th annual July 4th parade, followed by a family picnic in Edgemont Park and a fireworks display at Yogi Berra Stadium on the Montclair State University campus. Hours: Parade begins at 11 a.m., followed by the family picnic; fireworks begin around sundown. Go: Parade begins at South Fullerton Avenue and Bloomfield Avenue and travels to Edgemont Park; Edgemont Park, Valley Road and Holland Terrace, Montclair.

Newark

The Essex County Free Summer Concert Series will include two free performances in Newark featuring fireworks displays. Hours: Both concerts begin at 7:30 p.m.

The New Jersey Symphony Orchestra will perform on June 28. The program will feature a medley of classics, Broadway themes and patriotic favorites; as well as John Williams’ Liberty Fanfare, John Philip Sousa’s Atlantic City Pageant March and other Jersey treasures. Go: The Great Lawn at Branch Brook Park, Heller Parkway. In case of rain, the concert will be relocated to the Jim Wise Theatre in Kupfrian Hall on Summit Street on the campus of NJIT.

Men of Soul will perform soul and R&B music on July 2. Go: Weequahic Park, Elizabeth and Meeker avenues.

Nutley

Nutley Fourth of July Celebration and Fireworks. In Nutley, July 4th festivities include a variety of food vendors, liv music, games and a fireworks show. Hours: Celebration events start at 6:30 p.m. and fireworks begin at dusk. Go: Nutley Park Oval, 300 Franklin Ave. Nutley.

Verona

Verona Fourth of July Fireworks. Verona's Fourth of July event on June 28 will include a night full of dancing with a DJ and other live entertainment, as well as a fireworks show at dusk. Hours: Starts at 7 pm. Go: Verona Community Center, 880 Bloomfield Ave., Verona.

Hudson County

Jersey City

Jersey City 4th of July Celebrations. At Exchange Place Path Plaza, there will be a variety of activities on July 4th, include the Jersey City Night Market, carnival rides, games, live music and food vendors. Then, enjoy the annual Macy's July 4th fireworks on the Hudson River. Hours: Noon to 10 p.m. Go: 68 Christopher Columbus Drive, Jersey City.

title: Broadway: Home revival written by Samm-Art-Williams-died
fullText:
The first Broadway revival of Samm-Art Williams’ “Home” is full of joy and pain, heart and hope.

And sorrow, for the playwright passed away days before the first preview. But rest assured Williams is smiling from above after every performance, for this atypical work is engrossing and entertaining  

The story is about Cephus Miles (Tory Kittles), a Black farmer in North Carolina. He’s in love with Pattie Mae (Brittany Inge), who goes off to college. But things take a turn when he is thrown in jail for opposing the Vietnam War draft. And when he moves to the big city, his life becomes dangerous and complicated.

Directed by the Tony Award-winning Kenny Leon, the script in this 90-minute show is packed with poetry, melody, rhythm and song.

There's talk of land, soil, sun, rain and crops.

God, faith and family — and America.

There are dozens of characters, but only three people in this small-scale but mighty production. The acting is first-rate. Stori Ayers is identified as Woman Two in the program, but she portrays everyone from a a youngster to a prison guard to a bus driver. Watching her transform from one moment to the next is one of the highlights of the night.

The audience warms up to Kittles quickly. He allows us to share Cephus' tragedy as he goes from the comforts of home to jail to being lost among the masses, peddling for cash any way he can.

Inge plays multiple characters, too, but she shines bright as Pattie Mae. Maybe it's her eyes? Her smile? There's real chemistry between Inge and Kittles that is wonderful to see.

The minimal set by Arnulfo Maldonado works, as does lighting by Allen Lee Hughes, costumes by Dede Ayite, sound design by Justin Ellington, and hair and wig design by Nikiya Mathis. Kate Wilson deserves mention as voice coach.  

Everything comes together to make this a feel-good evening. The ending may be predictable, but that’s OK.

“Home” opens the 2024-25 season, and it’s timing could not be better. What are the tens of thousands of migrants looking for? Jobs, opportunities, a place to start again.

The work also gives voice to the poor and lonely and homeless — and anyone in America looking for a place to fit in, to belong.

And it's a reminder that no matter how far away we go, we can’t escape who we are, where we come from.

Home will always be a part of us.

Go: “Home,” through July 21, Todd Haimes Theatre, 227 W. 42nd St., New York, $49 to $149; 212-719-1300, roundabouttheatre.org.

Bill Canacci can be reached at bcanacci@gannettnj.com.

prompt: What is the Broadway revival of Home about, and how are critics reacting to Kenny Leon's new production?
response_text:
The Broadway revival of Home is a lyrical, bittersweet story about a Black man's search for belonging, love, and a place he can truly call his own. Directed by Tony Award winner Kenny Leon, the production brought Samm-Art Williams’s 1979 play back to Broadway for the first time in more than 40 years. It opened on June 5, 2024, at Roundabout Theatre Company's Todd Haimes Theatre.

Playbill
+1

What is Home about?

8

The play follows Cephus Miles, a young Black farmer from rural Cross Roads, North Carolina, played by Tory Kittles.

Cephus begins with a deep attachment to his land, his community, and his childhood sweetheart, Pattie Mae Wells. But his life gradually unravels:

  • Loss and heartbreak: After family tragedies, Pattie Mae leaves for college and eventually marries someone else.

  • Conscience and punishment: Cephus refuses to serve in the Vietnam War on religious grounds and goes to prison as a draft resister.

  • Disillusionment up North: After his release, he moves to the city, where he struggles with loneliness, drugs, and the feeling that he has lost his way.

  • The meaning of home: Ultimately, he must decide what home really means and whether he can recover the sense of belonging he once had.

The story is told through Cephus's direct address to the audience, poetic language, humor, and the work of three actors who bring dozens of characters to life. Although it confronts racism, incarceration, and hardship, it is ultimately a hopeful story about resilience and the possibility of returning to one's roots.

New York Stage Review
+2

How are critics reacting to Kenny Leon's production?

The critical response was mixed to positive. Reviewers generally admired the play's poetic writing and the cast's performances, but some felt Leon's brisk direction and the production's sentimental tone softened its more challenging themes.

What critics praised

  • Tory Kittles's central performance: Reviewers highlighted his charisma and his ability to portray Cephus across different stages of life.

  • The language: Williams's rhythmic, lyrical dialogue was frequently singled out as the play's greatest strength.

  • The emotional payoff: Several critics found the homecoming moving and uplifting, even when its outcome was predictable.

The Wall Street Journal praised the acting and the richness of Williams's language; Time Out also found that the play ultimately won its audience over.

The Wall Street Journal
+1

What critics questioned

  • The pacing: The New York Times and Wall Street Journal noted that the rapid-fire delivery sometimes made the dense dialogue and shifting chronology difficult to follow.

  • The staging: Some reviewers thought the relatively spare set and intimate theatrical approach did not fully fill the large Broadway venue.

  • The softened edges: Vulture argued that Leon's production leaned too heavily into sentimentality, leaving some of the script's unresolved tensions underexplored.

BroadwayWorld
+2

The overall verdict

Critics largely saw Home as a worthwhile revival of an important work of Black American theatre, rather than a universally successful production. Leon's energetic approach gives the play momentum, and the performers bring warmth and humor to Cephus's journey. However, that same speed can obscure Williams's poetic language and diminish the weight of the play's darker experiences.

The revival also took on additional poignancy because Williams died in May 2024, shortly before previews began. For some reviewers, the production served as a heartfelt tribute to the playwright and his legacy.

New York Stage Review
+1

One important detail: this was a limited engagement that closed in July 2024, so these reviews concern that specific production, not a currently running Broadway show.

title: See results of Ramapo, Indian Hills enrollment disparity study
fullText:
OAKLAND — The Ramapo Indian Hills School District will struggle for the next five years to recover from a slump in student enrollment.

The information, which also shows more students are choosing to attend Ramapo High School over Indian Hills High School, comes from a Statistical Forecasting LLC demographic study that also found there is no foreseeable change in the uneven distribution of students between the district's two high schools — Indian Hills and Ramapo.

The results of the 59-page, $11,300 study were presented to the district's school board at the end of May by Richard Grip, owner of the Boston-based firm.

The study was called for in a five-year strategic plan proposed by former School Superintendent Rui Dionisio in June 2023. The goal was to address an ongoing imbalance of attendance between the two schools that affects the district's ability to deliver curriculum equally and how it affects its extracurricular activities, particularly sports.

Grip conceded that "we don't have an answer" for why students prefer one school over the other, or how to correct the imbalance. A separate study by the district is reportedly exploring those questions. Instead, his report offers a detailed statistical profile of the three municipalities.

The choice issue

The Ramapo Indian Hills Regional High School district's two schools serve ninth- through 12th-grade students from Franklin Lakes, Oakland and Wyckoff. Ramapo High School is located in Franklin Lakes and Indian Hills in Oakland.

Ramapo opened in January 1957 with 655 students. Indian Hills opened in September 1965 with 575 students. From 1971 to 1999, Franklin Lakes students were split geographically between the two high schools. Those east of the Franklin Lakes attended Ramapo High School and those west of the Franklin Lakes attended Indian Hills.

The Board of Education voted to end the Franklin Lakes "split" in January 1998 allowing students to choose either Ramapo or Indian Hills without geographic restriction starting in September 1999. The choice was extended to Oakland students in 2005. There is some debate when Wyckoff students were granted school choice, but all three districts now allow students to choose which school they attend.

The removal of choice restrictions was predicted to have an immediate negative impact on Indian Hills enrollment, but the shift happened more gradually.

In 2020, the question was raised whether the New Jersey State Interscholastic Athletic Association should reclassify the two schools given their enrollment and performance. Indian Hills was eyed for movement from Group 3 to Group 2 but no change has been made. Indian Hills fielded the dominant teams in the 1960s to the 1990s, but access to Ramapo's larger student base has allowed its teams to bypass Indian Hills on sports performance in recent years.

The size of each school's population also affects what classes and how many sections of those classes are offered, even the size of their marching bands. Most recently, the school board debated whether a dance team organized at Ramapo should include Indian Hills students, or require them to wait until they had sufficient numbers to justify a separate group.

Report highlights

The report provides statistical data on the three municipalities but does not attempt to analyze how this data plays into school choice.

  • Location: One of the simplest factors students may consider when choosing schools is the distance from their home. Franklin Lakes sits in the middle between Indian Hills in Oakland on its western border and Ramapo near its eastern border with Wyckoff. The 3.6 miles between the two schools may be a deciding factor, particularly for Oakland and Wyckoff students.
  • Capacity: According to the study, Ramapo High School can hold 1,663 students and is now operating at 72% capacity with 1,192 students, expected to drop slightly to 1,158 students (70% capacity) by the 2028-29 school year. Indian Hills can hold 1,469 students and is now operating at 48% capacity with 699 students, expected to increase slightly to 726 students (49% capacity) by the 2028-29 school year. There was no statistical breakdown by town which students attend which school.
  • Housing: The study says that from 2008 to 2011, housing sales declined in the area "due to the housing market crash and banking crisis." As a result, potential homeowners sought less pricey places to move. Students born during that slump living in one of the three towns are now ages 13 to 16. Student populations are expected to bottom out in 2024-2025 before a gradual upturn.
  • Two schools: Neither school is large enough to hold all students from both schools.
  • More homes: New home construction would be the most likely way to add new students. The study cites the Cigna 495-unit affordable housing development in Franklin Lakes as the most likely to produce a substantial number of new students. A 191-unit townhouse/apartment complex is also under construction next to Indian Hills on McCoy Road in Oakland. However, the study says since the units are not yet built and occupied, the impact of any children in these developments on the two schools is "outside the five-year enrollment projection timeframe."
  • Wealth culture: One of the ongoing arguments to explain the imbalance in student populations between the two schools has been that Franklin Lakes and Wyckoff share more socio-economic similarities than Oakland, and favor Ramapo High School as a result. The study provides facts about the area's economy, but draws no conclusions about the impact on school choice.
  • Median household income: Franklin Lakes $204,917, Wyckoff $184,858, Oakland $162,848, New Jersey overall $96,346.
  • Owner-occupied units: Franklin Lakes 3,258 (87.5%), Wyckoff 5,138 (92.3%), Oakland 3,974 (91.2%), New Jersey overall 61.3%.
  • Median value of owner-occupied unit (housing): Franklin Lakes $1,135,700, Wyckoff $885,400, Oakland $535,900, New Jersey overall $428,900.
  • Race (top two categories): Franklin Lakes: white 8,755 (79%), Asian 1,051 (9.5%); Wyckoff: white 13,767 (83%), Hispanic 1,315 (7.9%); Oakland: white 10,370 (81.3%), 1,210 Hispanic (9.5%).
  • Education: Percent of residents with bachelor degrees: Franklin Lakes 77.3%, Wyckoff 64.1%, Oakland 54.2%. Percent of residents with graduate or professional degrees: Franklin Lakes 35.8%, Wyckoff 28.1%, Oakland 20.9%.

prompt: What did the recent enrollment disparity study for the Ramapo Indian Hills Regional School District reveal about student numbers?
response_text:
The recent enrollment disparity study for the Ramapo Indian Hills Regional High School District found a significant imbalance in student populations between its two high schools: Ramapo High School had substantially more students than Indian Hills High School, even as overall district enrollment was declining. The district's March 2024 demographic study documented this trend.

rih.org
+1

Key findings

  • Ramapo High School: 1,663 students, operating at approximately 72% of capacity.

  • Indian Hills High School: 699 students, operating at approximately 48% of capacity.

  • Enrollment gap: Ramapo had 964 more students than Indian Hills — more than twice Indian Hills' enrollment.

    AOL

The longer-term figures in the study showed that the disparity had widened considerably:

  • Indian Hills: Enrollment fell 43% between 2014–15 and 2023–24, from 1,225 to about 699 students.

  • Ramapo: Enrollment increased by about 10% over the same period, from 1,088 to 1,192 students, before beginning to decline.

  • Districtwide: Total enrollment fell 18.3%, from 2,313 to about 1,891 students.

    archive.rih.org

title: NJ university police sergeant charged in fraud scheme gets PTI
fullText:
A 25-year veteran Montclair State University police sergeant accused of trading his PBA card for forged insurance documents has entered a diversionary court program to resolve the charges against him.

Christopher Angst, 49, of Long Valley, avoided jail time during a hearing last week in state Superior Court, but was required to forfeit his employment at the state's second largest public university, where he had been employed as a police officer since 1999, according to pension records.

Angst, who was charged in 2023 on third- and fourth-degree charges including insurance fraud, forgery and falsifying/tampering with records, agreed to the terms of the pretrial intervention program on June 17 before Judge Ralph Amirata, a state Superior Court judge in Morris County.

Following successful completion of a 12-month probationary term, the charges against Angst will be dismissed, Amirata stated. Angst is also barred from future public employment, including as a police officer.

Prosecutors accused Angst of conspiring with Michael McFadden, 54, of New Milford, an insurance agent with Insuranze Associates in Hasbrouck Heights, charging the men via summonses in September 2023, according to the Morris County Prosecutor's Office.

Morris County NJ Former NJ assemblywoman files $15M whistleblower lawsuit against Dover, mayor

McFadden allegedly created false documents saying Angst had a workers' compensation coverage policy for his company, C&E Professional Painting LLC, in Long Valley. The business did not have a workers' compensation policy, officials said.

Angst had allegedly falsely presented his company to a client as being insured and the client unknowingly submitted the fake documents to an insurance carrier, according to officials.

Angst was also accused of gifting McFadden a gold Police Benevolent Association card in exchange for the documents, authorities said.

Angst did not admit guilt during the short court hearing and will be monitored by the court and undergo various programs for rehabilitation through the pretrial intervention program, or PTI, which is offered to first-time offenders based on a number of statutory guidelines.

Angst was initially charged with one count of fourth-degree falsifying/tampering with records, one count of third-degree insurance fraud, one count of fourth-degree failure to provide workers' compensation, one count of fourth-degree forgery, and one count of third-degree conspiracy to commit insurance fraud.

McFadden is facing charges of fourth-degree falsifying, one count of third-degree insurance fraud, one count of fourth-degree hindering, one count of fourth-degree forgery, and one count of third-degree conspiracy to commit insurance fraud. His charges have yet to be resolved.

Angst, who was represented by attorney Roy Breslow, agreed to provide a sworn statement and truthful testimony for future court hearings.

title: Morris Knolls softball claims second straight state sectional title
fullText:
DENVILLE – All Julia Fox was thinking was to keep it simple.

With leadoff batter and teammate Taylor Heinemann standing on third base with one out in the first inning, the Morris Knolls sophomore was focused on hitting a shot deep enough to the outfield to help her team in the biggest game of the season.

Facing a 2-1 hitter’s count, Fox’s sacrifice fly to right field plated Heinemann in what turned out to be the only run of the game to lift Morris Knolls to a 1-0 victory over rival Morris Hills on Saturday in the NJSIAA North 1, Group 3 final. It’s the Golden Eagles second straight sectional title.

Senior pitcher Leah Kleczkowski spun a three-hit, complete game shutout with six strikeouts to lead the Denville school to its sixth straight win.

Morris Knolls will host Randolph in a Group 3 semifinal on Tuesday. Randolph defeated North Hunterdon, 8-3 on Saturday in the North 2, Group 3 final.

“I was looking for a sacrifice fly. I just knew that I didn’t want to pop up in the infield because I knew Taylor and that run could be really crucial,” Fox said. “It’s a great feeling to win again. The whole team plays really well together. It’s not too often you get to experience something like this.”

Heinemann came out swinging in the bottom half of the first inning and reached second base when she laced a fly ball to left field on a 2-1 count that tailed away and ended up scored an error. She then stole third just ahead of Fox’s plate appearance.

“I just made sure that I got back to the base in time and run as fast to home and make sure I was safe,” Heinemann said. “We’ve put in a lot of work this season and it’s nice to win it again.”

The Golden Eagles could only string together two hits - singles from Makayla Rady in the third and Hailey Poskonka in the fifth - but tight defense and a big-game effort by Kleczkowski was enough to hold it down.

Morris Hills (15-13) threatened in the sixth inning when its first two batters reached base, giving the Scarlet Knights runners on first and second with no outs. But the Golden Eagles defense buckled down and Kleczkowski induced the next two batters to pop up in the infield and a ground out.

“I’m not surprised it was only a one-run game. I wish it was bigger, but I knew it was going to be a tight game. They [Morris Hills] always put up a good fight. I’m glad we won,” Kleczkowski  said. “Winning by a run is still a win. We’ve prepared all season for this moment. It’s a great feeling knowing the hard work is paying off.”

Morris Hills pitcher Zoe Turner was impressive, going six innings on two hits and no runs.

What it means

Morris Knolls (23-4) is state sectional champions for the second straight year. They’ve reached a sectional final three straight times.

In their four postseason games, the Golden Eagles have only surrendered one run. Morris Knolls has outscored its opponents, 21-1 with three shutouts.,

The Golden Eagles face county and division rival Randolph (20-8) next in a Group 3 semifinal on Tuesday. Morris Knolls defeated the Rams twice during the regular season and have outscored them, 14-3.

“This year we’re just a little more experienced compared to last year. We’re just a year older,” Morris Knolls coach Keith Heinemann said. “Leah has been fantastic this whole tournament. Their [Morris Hills] pitching did a great job and kept us off the bases. We’re still alive.”

They said it

“Whenever we play [Morris] Hills, no matter the sport, it’s always an intense game. Our whole motto this season is ‘nothing is given, everything is earned.’ We knew we had to come out, compete and do our jobs. We knew it was going to be a battle. I felt prepared and confident because I have a very strong defense with good hitters behind me. It’s my senior year and you always want to end on a good note. I knew I could do it and I’m happy coach believed in me.” - Kleczkowski

“We knew today was going to be different than the last time we played them. Their coaches do a great job and they have some really good young talent. Their pitcher has been lights out all tournament, so we expected the challenge.” - Keith Heinemann

title: Buying an empty lot: Should you build a house on one?
fullText:
In the 1948 film, "Mr. Blandings Builds His Dream House," a family decides to move from their cramped New York apartment to a grand farmhouse in need of renovation in Connecticut. But after buying the property, they realize the home is structurally unsound and must be torn down. Now, left with nothing but a vacant lot, the family faces a whole slew of problems as they try to build their new home.

If you're a potential homebuyer weighing whether it's worth buying a cheap vacant lot and building your own home, rather than fighting the masses for what few existing and pricey properties are available in North Jersey, you might want to give this film a watch.

Opting for a vacant lot and starting your home from scratch might sound like an ideal alternative to navigating today's market, but it will more than likely be the opposite: A project that will end up being both more time consuming and more expensive in the long run.

"I think the dream of homeownership is very alive, and obviously the demand and housing market is there," said Derek Weissman, partner and head of asset management at Procida Funding & Advisors in Englewood Cliffs. "I still think there's a desire to develop and design something yourself, and there's a belief that it can be done quicker or more efficiently. But, unfortunately, a lot of people are running into cost overruns and time constraints, or projects are going a lot longer than they anticipate."

While determining which option is more expensive can be complicated, there's more that goes into building a new home that you may not have considered.

The cost, and availability, of materials and labor

As of early June, empty lots with as much as a quarter of an acre of land — approximately the average lot size in New Jersey, give or take — are available throughout the state for anywhere from $4,000 to $9 million, depending on the area.

Besides this, the second biggest factor people consider when determining whether it's worth building a home on a vacant lot is the cost and availability of both materials and labor. According to a May 2024 report from Bankrate, the total cost of things like framing, foundation, roofing and painting alone can cost as much as $272,840, depending on the size of the house, the cost of labor and the type of materials used.

Weissman said that when you're in the process of building, you'll also likely make several changes to the project as the home comes to life, which will only increase the costs.

"You end up getting engaged with picking out your cabinets, your finishes, your appliances, your bathroom colors and things like that," he said. "But, also understand, once your start making these selections, it's like anything in life. When you a la carte it, it gets a lot more expensive. So, I recommended to any of our clients, if you're going to build your own home, add in at least a 15% to 20% contingency. That may be a touch high, but it's always better to come in under the budget you give yourself, and the last thing you want it to start building your home and then run into this problem where you run out of money because you overspent on the bathroom and now you can't put the cabinets in the kitchen."

The time and price of setting up utilities

Depending on where an empty lot is located, you'll more than likely have to use both time and money setting up utility services to the lot. According to Bankrate, the cost of setting up things like plumbing, electrical wiring and HVAC in the home once it's built can cost $32,500 or more. And, there will be additional costs to have utility services run to your lot, if they aren't already, in the first place.

In addition to the price of doing this, Weissman said waiting for materials to become available and then waiting while it gets installed will take a lot of time. For example, he said his company has a current client who has been waiting for a water connection for about four weeks. In another project, he said the buyer had to wait for electrical switch gear for more than three weeks, and then it took anywhere from two to three months to install.

"I do think a lot of people are underestimating what public service timing is right now, and that can be water, sewer or electrical, and the components that go into water, sewer and electrical," Weissman said. "It's not just getting the timing from your local water authority or local electrical service provider, but it's also — are the materials that you need to put in the home readily available?"

The process of prepping the land for building

Weissman said that because there is also a scarcity in available land in New Jersey and throughout the Northeast, it's important to check that the lot is actually able to be built on. Because there is so little land available, there's a possibility that the land has existing conditions that would make it not suitable for residential building, or would result in extra time and money to remedy the lot for building.

In addition to checking if the lot has proper utility connection points, he said you have to look at the zoning guidelines of the lot. Then, you have to consider why the lot might not have been picked up by an industry professional already, especially given the scarcity of land available.

"Is there a reason why this lot hasn't been picked up by a house flipper or a more institutional-type investor looking to buy this and rent it, or buy this and flip it when the market's been as high as it is?" he said. "And then it comes down to why the lot is still siting there. What is the unknown? Is there an oil tank that I might have to radiate? Is there rock underneath that I'm going to have a hard time drawing into.

"As a novice homebuyer, someone who's not within the industry but is looking to come create the American Dream and build their single-family home, you sometimes don't dig as deep into what could be happening under the surface."

Financing for new construction is different

Getting the proper financing to build your own home is also different from if you were to buy an existing home.

As opposed to taking out a typical mortgage, you'd be required to take out a home construction loan, which is a short-term, higher-interest loan that would provide the money needed to build a residential property, according to Bankrate.

In order to be approved for a home construction loan, you must provide building plans, project timelines, financials and other documentation ahead of time, and the loan typically has a term of one year. During construction, borrowers typically pay interest, then the remaining balance will transition to a traditional mortgage after construction is finished.

"Generally, the most important thing is to not let emotion get to you. You're seeing right now that single-family homes in the entry-level range, which varies depending on where you are, are going up. You're seeing a list of people that are lined up looking to buy and you can't get beaten down if you lost 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 or more homes that you liked. Don't all the sudden jump and make a rash decision because of that, and just be willing to stay the course," he said.

"It's really important to make sure that this is a place that you're going to be able to call home for a long time. And, if you choose the alternative, and you find piece of dirt that you're able to build on, just make sure you understand the time it's going to take. Building a home is a very time consuming process, not only as you wait for the actual home to be built, but a lot of steps in the process."

seoTitle: Buying an empty lot: Should you build a house on one?
prompt: What important factors should I consider before buying and building a new home on vacant land in North Jersey?
response_text:
Buying vacant land and building a new home in North Jersey can be a great way to get the home you want, but it’s also a project where the land itself can make or break your budget. A lot that looks perfect on paper may turn out to be expensive to build on because of zoning restrictions, steep slopes, wetlands, septic requirements, drainage problems, or the cost of connecting utilities.

My biggest recommendation is to evaluate the property as a buildable homesite, not simply as a piece of land you like.

Here are the most important factors I would investigate before committing to a purchase.

1. Confirm that you can legally build the home you want

Zoning and permitted use

Contact the municipality's zoning officer or construction department before making an offer. Confirm:

  • Whether a single-family home is permitted as of right.

  • Minimum lot area, lot width, and frontage.

  • Front, side, and rear setbacks.

  • Maximum building height, lot coverage, and impervious surface limits.

  • Whether the property is a legally recognized lot or requires a variance or subdivision.

  • Whether deed restrictions, easements, or homeowners' association rules limit construction.

A lot advertised as residential is not necessarily buildable. An undersized lot, a narrow frontage, or an irregular shape can prevent you from building the home you envision.

What to request: A written zoning review and a preliminary site plan showing the proposed house, driveway, garage, and required setbacks.

2. Investigate wetlands, flood risk, and environmental restrictions

Environmental due diligence

North Jersey has wooded parcels, streams, wetlands, protected open space, and environmentally sensitive areas. These can substantially reduce the portion of a lot where construction is allowed.

Check for:

  • Freshwater wetlands and regulated transition areas.

  • Flood zones and local stormwater requirements.

  • Streams, drainage channels, and riparian buffers.

  • Steep slopes, rock outcroppings, and unstable soils.

  • Protected trees, endangered species habitat, or other conservation restrictions.

  • Former land uses that could have contaminated the soil.

Use FEMA flood maps and New Jersey environmental mapping as an initial screen, but don't rely on online maps alone. Depending on the parcel, you may need a wetlands delineation, survey, soil investigation, or environmental assessment.

Useful resources include the FEMA Flood Map Service Center  and the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection .

Important: A parcel can be outside a mapped flood zone and still have significant drainage or stormwater problems.

3. Determine the true cost of making the lot buildable

This is one of the biggest financial risks, especially on wooded, sloped, or undeveloped land.

Site expense

What can drive the cost up

Clearing and demolition

Dense trees, stumps, old foundations, buried debris

Excavation and grading

Slopes, retaining walls, difficult access

Rock removal

Shallow bedrock, blasting restrictions, hauling

Foundation

Poor soil, groundwater, deep foundations

Drainage and stormwater

Detention systems, infiltration systems, extensive piping

Driveway and access

Long driveway, steep grade, culverts, road improvements

Utility connections

Long distances to water, sewer, gas, or electric

Engineering and approvals

Surveys, soil tests, permits, specialized studies

A cheap lot may ultimately cost more than a more expensive lot that is already cleared, serviced, and approved for construction.

My advice: Get a preliminary site-development estimate from a local civil engineer and a builder before your inspection or feasibility period expires. Don't base the budget on the cost of the house alone.

4. Verify water, sewer, septic, and other utilities

Before buying, establish exactly how the property will be serviced.

  • Public water and sewer: Confirm that service is available at the property, that capacity exists, and what connection, tap, assessment, and extension fees apply.

  • Private well: If public water is unavailable, investigate well feasibility, water quality testing, drilling costs, and applicable permits.

  • Septic system: If there is no public sewer, confirm that the soil and site can support an approved septic system sized for your intended home. A soil evaluation and required septic testing may be necessary.

  • Electricity and gas: Obtain estimates for extending service, installing transformers, or using alternatives such as propane or electric heating.

  • Internet: Verify actual service availability rather than assuming nearby homes have the same options.

  • Stormwater drainage: Determine how roof runoff, driveway runoff, and groundwater will be handled without violating local or state requirements.

In New Jersey, local health departments generally oversee residential septic approvals, and additional NJDEP approvals may be necessary when wetlands or other regulated areas are involved. See the NJDEP septic permitting guidance .

Permitting Information
+1

A key question to ask: Are utilities already connected to this lot, merely available in the street, or not available at all? Those are three very different cost situations.

5. Get a survey and investigate access and title

A real estate listing or tax map isn't sufficient to establish the property's exact boundaries or usable area.

Have a New Jersey-licensed land surveyor evaluate the parcel and, as appropriate, provide:

  • A current boundary survey with property lines and monuments.

  • A topographic survey showing elevations, contours, and significant site features.

  • The location of existing easements, rights-of-way, utilities, and encroachments.

  • Confirmation of legal frontage and access to a public road or a properly documented private road.

Have a real estate attorney review the title commitment, deed restrictions, utility easements, shared driveways, road-maintenance agreements, and any recorded limitations on development.

Pay particular attention to legal access. A driveway that physically exists does not necessarily mean you have a permanent legal right to use it. You may also need municipal approval for a new driveway entrance or curb cut.

6. Understand the North Jersey location-specific risks

North Jersey isn't one uniform real estate market. Conditions can differ substantially between Bergen, Passaic, Morris, Essex, Sussex, and Warren counties, and even between neighboring towns.

Bergen and eastern Passaic counties

Look closely at lot coverage, setbacks, stormwater requirements, tree-removal rules, neighboring property constraints, and the cost of building in established neighborhoods. Small or irregular lots may sharply limit house design.

Morris and western Passaic counties

Investigate slopes, shallow bedrock, retaining walls, drainage, and wetlands. Check whether Highlands-related regulations or local environmental ordinances apply to the specific property.

Sussex and Warren counties

Rural parcels may offer more space, but evaluate well and septic feasibility, long utility runs, driveway construction, winter access, and the cost of clearing and grading. Don't assume a large acreage guarantees a usable building site.

If a property is affected by the Highlands, wetlands, flood hazard, or other regulated areas, confirm which rules and permits apply to that specific parcel. The NJDEP's single-family home guidance  is a useful starting point.

Single Family Home
+1

Also investigate the practical aspects of daily living: commuting times, train access, school districts, property taxes, emergency services, road maintenance, and proximity to shopping and healthcare.

7. Calculate the complete project budget

Don't compare land prices and house construction prices separately. Calculate the total cost to move into a finished home.

Here's an illustrative planning budget for a custom home in North Jersey. These are example allowances, not contractor quotes or estimates for a particular parcel.

Budget item

Illustrative allowance

Vacant land purchase

$250,000

Site preparation, grading, driveway, drainage

$100,000

House construction

$700,000

Architecture, engineering, surveys, permits

$75,000

Utility connections and site-related fees

$40,000

Landscaping, appliances, and finishing items

$35,000

Contingency reserve

$95,000

Illustrative total

$1,295,000

The example assumes a $700,000 construction budget, with a contingency reserve of roughly 8% of the subtotal before contingency. Actual costs can be much lower or considerably higher depending on the home, town, and land conditions.

Make sure the budget clarifies whether the builder's quote includes:

  • Excavation, foundation, and rock removal.

  • Utility connections and impact or connection fees.

  • Driveway, retaining walls, drainage, and erosion control.

  • Landscaping, patios, decks, and fencing.

  • Appliances, lighting fixtures, and finish upgrades.

  • Architect and engineering fees, permits, and inspections.

  • Temporary utilities, construction insurance, and financing costs.

  • Final grading, certificates, and occupancy approvals.

Ask builders to separate fixed-price items, allowances, and exclusions. An attractive base price can be misleading if substantial site work and finishing costs are excluded.

8. Arrange financing before you buy the land

Financing a land purchase and a custom home build is different from obtaining a standard mortgage on an existing house.

Common options include:

  • Cash purchase of land: Gives you control over the parcel but ties up capital before construction begins.

  • Land loan: May require a larger down payment, a shorter term, or a higher interest rate than a conventional mortgage.

  • Construction loan: Funds construction in stages as work is completed.

  • Construction-to-permanent loan: Can combine construction financing and the eventual mortgage into one financing arrangement, subject to lender requirements.

Before closing, ask lenders:

  • How much cash must you contribute toward the land and construction?

  • Can your land equity count toward the required down payment?

  • When are construction funds disbursed?

  • What interest payments are due during construction?

  • What happens if the project exceeds its budget or schedule?

  • Does the loan require an approved builder, completed plans, permits, or a fixed-price contract?

Keep enough liquidity to cover unexpected expenses, interest payments, and potential delays. Don't use every dollar of your available funds to buy the lot.

9. Choose the builder and architect early

One common mistake is buying land first and figuring out the house later.

A better sequence is to identify a builder and architect who understand the town where you want to build, then have them evaluate the property before you purchase it.

Ask prospective builders for:

  • References from recently completed homes in North Jersey.

  • Experience obtaining approvals in the target municipality.

  • Evidence of appropriate insurance and applicable licenses or registrations.

  • A detailed estimate based on your intended home size and finish level.

  • A realistic construction schedule and process for handling change orders.

  • A clear warranty and written procedures for addressing defects.

Also consider whether you want a fully custom architect-designed home or a more standardized builder-designed home. A custom home offers greater flexibility but typically involves more design decisions, coordination, and potential cost uncertainty.

10. Protect yourself with contract contingencies

This is especially important when purchasing vacant land.

Have a New Jersey real estate attorney draft or review the purchase agreement before you commit. Negotiate a due-diligence period long enough to obtain meaningful answers from the municipality and qualified professionals.

Where appropriate, make the purchase contingent on satisfactory results for:

  • Zoning and confirmation of the intended residential use.

  • Survey and title review.

  • Wetlands, flood hazard, and environmental review.

  • Soil testing, septic feasibility, or well feasibility.

  • Utility availability and connection costs.

  • Driveway access and other required approvals.

  • Financing and the feasibility of the proposed construction budget.

If the project requires variances or environmental permits, understand that obtaining them may take months, may require public hearings, and may not be guaranteed.

Do not rely solely on a seller's statement that the lot is buildable. Verify the claim independently. If you need a variance or other discretionary approval, the contract should specifically address the risk of that approval being denied.

11. Account for property taxes, insurance, and long-term value

Your carrying costs won't stop once the house is complete.

  • Property taxes: Ask the municipality or tax assessor how the land is currently assessed and how a newly constructed home may affect the assessment. Build a realistic estimate into your monthly housing costs.

  • Construction insurance: Verify builder's risk coverage, liability insurance, and responsibility for damage or theft during construction.

  • Homeowners insurance: Check whether the location, roof design, tree exposure, flood risk, or distance from emergency services affects coverage or premiums.

  • Resale value: Compare your expected total project cost with completed homes in the immediate area, not just land prices or aspirational listings.

  • Neighborhood restrictions: Consider whether future nearby development, road changes, or conservation restrictions could affect privacy, access, and value.

A beautiful custom home can still be a poor investment if the total cost substantially exceeds what buyers in that location are likely to pay.

12. Follow this order before committing

Your vacant-land due-diligence checklist

Use this checklist as you evaluate a specific parcel.

0 of 10 completed

My bottom line

The three things I would prioritize above everything else are:

  1. Prove the lot is buildable under the applicable zoning and environmental rules.

  2. Establish the true site-development cost before agreeing to the purchase price.

  3. Protect your ability to walk away if the property fails your feasibility tests.

A little extra diligence before closing can prevent a costly mistake that is difficult or impossible to reverse after you own the land.

title: Could the NJ skyline rise to meet NY skyscrapers? Expert thinks so
fullText:
Jason Barr has studied Manhattan skyscrapers since he joined the Rutgers-Newark faculty in 2003, but he believes towering future changes to the skyline will become more prevalent across the Hudson River — in New Jersey.

Barr grew up in the suburbs on Long Island and had no interest in skyscrapers, not until he stumbled across a database, Emporis.com, on tall buildings around the world. 

Story continues below photo gallery

After he became fascinated by the history of skyscrapers in New York, Barr started researching them — what drove their height, how many were built, and more. “Skyscrapers made Manhattan Manhattan,” said Barr, now an expert on the economics of skyscrapers.

His new book, "Cities in the Sky: The Quest to Build the World's Tallest Skyscrapers," just came out in May. His book "Building the Skyline: The Birth and Growth of Manhattan’s Skyscrapers," was released in 2016. He also currently writes the Skynomics Blog about skyscrapers, cities, and economics.

More: NJ Transit to gain revenue from new housing at Metropark station. A recipe for elsewhere?

More: COVID was a final blow to some NJ suburban office parks. Here's how they're morphing

Barr’s favorite skyscraper is the Empire State Building. “Every city looks to the Empire State Building as the building that sets the mold," he said. "Other countries want their own Empire State Building.”  

Transit-focused towers for New Jersey

Now, Barr is looking at the future of skyscrapers, with New Jersey at the forefront. “The best strategy is for all cities and towns along NJ Transit lines to build apartment buildings,” said Barr, who believes transit-oriented buildings would benefit New Jersey communities. 

Many new residential buildings have already started to crop up by NJ Transit stations, including in urban Orange and East Orange, and in suburban towns as well. Planners call these communities transit hubs.

Barr says there is still a lot of room for cities in New Jersey to grow. “The old historical cities like Jersey City and Newark have a lot of old vacant land from factories, and are willing to exploit that,” he said. Barr believes more buildings would attract many people and boost economic activity. 

Jersey City always pitched itself as a Manhattan alternative, Barr said, and has an opportunity to follow through on that goal. “New York City is so expensive," he said. "There’s a lot of issues with zoning and difficulty in building. People go to Jersey when New York gets expensive.”

Barr said Manhattan would have expanded west if not for the Hudson River. Now, Jersey City has the opportunity to finish what New York started by building more of their own skyscrapers.

prompt: Why do skyscraper experts believe that New Jersey will see an increase in high-rises driven by development trends near Manhattan?
response_text:
Skyscraper experts expect New Jersey to see more high-rise development because growth and housing demand are spilling across the Hudson River from Manhattan into cities where building can be comparatively less expensive and developable land is more available. Jersey City and Hoboken are especially well positioned to benefit from this trend.

HVS
+1

Five reasons New Jersey's skyline is likely to grow

1. Manhattan's influence is spreading west

People and businesses want access to New York City's jobs, culture, and financial center without necessarily paying Manhattan prices. New Jersey's waterfront cities offer proximity to the same economic hub, making them attractive locations for apartments, offices, and mixed-use towers.

HVS
+1

2. Transit makes high-density development practical

The PATH train connects Jersey City and Hoboken with Manhattan. Developers can build large residential communities near stations, allowing residents to commute without relying entirely on cars. As prime waterfront sites fill up, transit-oriented neighborhoods such as Journal Square are becoming important growth areas.

HVS
+1

3. Development economics can favor New Jersey

Lower development costs and greater land availability can make some projects more financially viable than comparable projects in New York City. Redevelopment of parking lots, former industrial sites, and underused parcels also gives developers opportunities to build taller, denser projects.

HVS
+1

4. Developers see demand for urban living

New Jersey is attracting renters and buyers seeking modern apartments, amenities, waterfront views, and convenient commutes. Industry participants have pointed to substantial leasing demand and the region's large population as reasons for continued investment, although high vacancy and oversupply remain risks in some areas.

New Jersey Business News
+1

5. One successful tower encourages the next

Once developers establish that large projects can attract tenants and buyers, additional projects become easier to justify. This creates a cycle of investment, new retail and amenities, and more residential development that can gradually transform entire districts.

New Jersey Business News
+1

What this looks like on the ground

Recent projects illustrate how quickly this trend is taking shape:

  • Jersey City: A proposed development at 310 Washington Street includes three towers of 50–57 stories, with more than 2,000 planned residences.

    KPF

  • Journal Square: Large residential projects are extending high-rise development beyond the immediate waterfront, supported by PATH access to Manhattan.

    HVS
    +1

  • Hoboken: The Hoboken Connect redevelopment includes a 27-story residential building, demonstrating that the trend is spreading to other transit-connected communities.

    Real Estate NJ

Will the growth continue indefinitely?

Not necessarily. Experts' expectations depend on interest rates, construction costs, rental demand, zoning approvals, and the ability of local infrastructure to support more residents. A 2026 multifamily market forecast also warns that thousands of new apartments arriving in Jersey City could put upward pressure on vacancies.

Institutional Property Advisors

The bottom line: New Jersey is increasingly functioning as an extension of the New York metropolitan urban core. Manhattan's economic pull, transit connectivity, housing demand, and development opportunities are encouraging more skyscrapers across the river.
